evidence.source: Shuowen Jiezi, via Chinese Text Project
evidence.text: The text gives separate entries: 号 is “a sound of pain,” formed from 口 above 丂; 號 is “to call,” formed from 号 and 虎. This is a historical lexicographic account, not independent confirmation of the pictured interpretation.
evidence.title: 說文解字 : 卷六 : 号部

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary reports that Shuowen treats 号 and 號 as separate head characters with somewhat different senses and pronunciations; later dictionaries mix them, and 号 came to be used as a variant of 號. It cites Dunhuang俗字譜 and later lexicons for forms and usage. This supports later graphic interchange, not an asserted single origin for both graphs.
evidence.title: [A03612] 號 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The Shuowen entry for 丂 explains it as breath wanting to emerge but obstructed above. This supports the historical semantic interpretation of the 丂 shape within 号; it does not establish 丂 as a phonetic element there.
evidence.title: [C00001] 丂 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.field: 號 Shuowen and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.text: The site gives Shuowen’s “呼也。从号从虎” and Duan Yucai’s account: the graph extends from shouting to name/title and command; 号 also serves as sound component, while 虎 contributes the idea of a loud, fierce cry. This is a later traditional analysis; the tiger-roar account is not independently demonstrated by the cited paleographic evidence inspected here.
evidence.title: 號 hào、háo - 漢典

evidence.field: 號 historical spellings and inscription catalogue
evidence.text: The entry lists bronze forms from the Western Zhou through early Spring and Autumn, a Shuowen seal form, Qin slips including Shuihudi 法98, and Han clerical examples. This indicates the compound graph is documented by Western Zhou bronze inscriptions in the displayed catalogue; no oracle-bone form is supplied there. The available page text does not establish the detailed graphic transitions or inspectable image readings.
evidence.title: 號 hào、háo - 漢典

evidence.text: The entry cites early textual examples for vocalization and crying, including the Book of Changes 同人 (“first cry, then laugh”) and Zhuangzi 養生主 (“three cries and left”), and for summoning/commanding cites Zuo zhuan 襄公十九年 and Zhuangzi 田子方. It cites Shiji and Han shu examples for naming/title and claiming a number. Textual work dates are not equivalent to dates of surviving manuscripts or inscriptions.
evidence.title: 號 hào、háo - 漢典

evidence.text: The dictionary reports Middle Chinese fanqie 胡刀切 for the level-tone reading and 胡到切 for the departing-tone reading; it labels them 匣母, 豪/号 rhyme, open grade I. It also gives Tang readings *hɑu and *hɑ̀u, modern Mandarin hào/háo, Cantonese hou4/hou6, Japanese readings, Korean ho, and Vietnamese hiệu. These readings concern 號 and its readings, not an independently reconstructed name for a depicted tiger cry.
evidence.title: 號 hào、háo - 漢典

evidence.text: This entry proposes a tiger with a line for exhaled air as an early ideogram, says later forms added 口 or 言, and analyzes modern 號 as 号 phonetic plus 虎 semantic. Its Zhengzhang Old Chinese values are 号 *ɦlaːws and 號 *ɦlaːw/*ɦlaːws, which make the proposed sound role plausible within that reconstruction. This is an attributed analysis, not direct proof of the original referent or the earliest graph; the entry's sequence conflicts with the Inscription catalogue inspected, which presents the graph as attested in Western Zhou bronze.
evidence.title: 號 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.text: The entry proposes an early tiger-plus-exhalation sign, later supplemented with 口 or 言, and says 号 derives from 口 plus 丂. This source’s detailed referent proposal is not corroborated by the inspected primary dictionary entry, which instead explains 号 as mouth over obstructed breath.
evidence.title: 號 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.text: The entry groups 號 and 号 in Zhengzhang’s 号 phonetic series, giving 号 *ɦlaːws and 號 *ɦlaːw/*ɦlaːws; its separate analysis of 号 as 口+丂 is not supported as a phonetic analysis. The external sources inspected do not establish that 丂 was a phonetic component of 号, so no sound component is assigned to 号 here.
evidence.title: 號 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.text: The entry gives the semantic chain shouting/calling → names or titles → commands and describes later senses such as signs, assigned order or number, aliases, horns, and a count classifier. Its cited samples range from classics such as Zuo zhuan and Shiji to later texts; this establishes dictionary-attested examples, not the first occurrence of each sense.
evidence.title: 號 hào、háo - 漢典

evidence.text: The entry lists 号 among the variant forms of 號. Combined with the MOE account of later interchange, this supports present-day 号 as the simplified graph used for 號, while retaining the older independent 号 graph in the separate historical tradition.
evidence.title: 號 hào、háo - 漢典

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary treats 号 and 號 as separate Shuowen head characters with somewhat different senses and readings, then describes later mixing: clerical writing commonly used 號 for 号, and later dictionaries increasingly conflated them. It cites the Dunhuang俗字譜, 玉篇, 廣韻 and other lexicons. This supports later graphic convergence, not one origin for both graphs.
evidence.title: [A03612] 號 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry quotes Shuowen: 號 means 呼 and is made from 号 and 虎, with fanqie 乎刀切. Its historical compilation account analyzes 虎 as semantic and 号 as carrying the sound; it also reports later senses/readings for calling, crying, and commanding. This is lexicographic testimony, not independent proof that the graph originated as a tiger-roar picture.
evidence.title: [A03612] 號 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry quotes Shuowen for 号 as a painful cry, formed from 口 above 丂. The page supports the traditional semantic interpretation of obstructed breath for 丂, but does not establish that 丂 is phonetic in 号.
evidence.title: [A03612] 號 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry quotes Shuowen's explanation of 丂 as breath wanting to emerge but obstructed above, and gives modern Mandarin kǎo with Shuowen fanqie 苦浩切. This is evidence about 丂 independently; it does not make 丂 a phonetic in 号.
evidence.title: [C00001] 丂 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.text: The entry cites early textual examples for crying and calling: 《易·同人》先號咷而後笑, 《莊子·養生主》三號而出, 《左傳·襄公十九年》號之乃下, and 《莊子·田子方》號於國中. It also cites 《史記》 for claiming a number and 《左傳·昭公四年》 for naming. These are dictionary-cited examples in works conventionally assigned early dates; they do not date surviving witnesses or establish the first occurrence of each sense.
evidence.title: 號 hào、háo - 漢典

evidence.text: The entry lists meanings including crying/shouting, animal or wind roaring, calling, ordering, names and aliases, signs, sequence numbers, horns and classifiers. Its citations and gloss organization suggest possible semantic links from calling to names and orders, but do not supply a complete dated history of those extensions.
evidence.title: 號 hào、háo - 漢典

evidence.text: The entry gives modern Mandarin hào/háo and Cantonese hou4/hou6. It reports Middle Chinese 匣母 豪韻 level 胡刀切 (Baxter haw; Zhengzhang /ɦɑu/) and departing 胡到切 (Baxter hawH; Zhengzhang /ɦɑuH/). These are readings of 號 and do not recover a historical tiger-call word.
evidence.title: 號 hào、háo - 漢典

evidence.source: Wiktionary, citing Zhengzhang Shangfang and Baxter–Sagart
evidence.text: For 號's háo reading it gives Middle Chinese haw, Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *[C.ɡ]ˤaw and Zhengzhang *ɦlaːw; for hào it gives hawH, *Cə.[ɡ]ˤaw-s and *ɦlaːws. The page explicitly treats 号 as 號's phonetic component in the Zhengzhang series. The page's 号 readings and 號 readings can be compared within those named systems, but these remain secondary transcriptions rather than an opened primary reconstruction dataset.
evidence.title: 號 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.field: 号 and 號 modern readings and reconstructions
evidence.text: The entry reports modern Mandarin háo and Middle Chinese haw for the cry/call reading; in Zhengzhang's 2003 system it gives 号 *ɦlaːw and 號 *ɦlaːw for one reading, and *ɦlaːws for the departing-tone call/order reading. This supports 号 as a plausible sound element in 號 within that system; it does not support 丂 as a phonetic component of the independent graph 号.
evidence.title: 號 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: 書法圖集, citing Shuowen and graph catalogues
evidence.field: 号 graph catalogue and dated form labels
evidence.text: The page labels forms of 号 from the Zenghouyi bells as early Warring States Chu bronze, a Shuowen 号部 form, and an Eastern Han Wuliang shrine inscription; it separately labels a Western Jin stele. Its Shuowen quotation gives 口 above 丂. These are catalogue labels, not direct dating evidence for the original graph, and the images are modern reproductions of historical forms.
evidence.title: 号字形演变 - 书法图集

evidence.text: The opened entry's catalogue lists 號 forms on Western Zhou bronzes including 同簋蓋 (集成4270), 𤼈壺 (集成9723), 鮮鐘 (集成143), and an early Spring and Autumn vessel. It also lists a Shuowen seal form, a Qin slip at 睡.法98, and Han clerical examples. This conflicts with the separate 号 graph's Warring States Chu form and means a general 'first appearance' claim needs graph-specific catalogue checking.
evidence.title: 號 hào、háo - 漢典

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry cites Dunhuang俗字譜 as commonly writing 號 with 号, and later dictionaries as mixing the forms and readings: háo for crying/pain and hào for command/call. It supports later graphic interchange and overlapping use, while preserving the distinction in the Shuowen record.

gaps: No external page was successfully opened for the Shuowen text itself; CText search-result excerpt supplies the two entries, and MOE reproduces them.

No oracle-bone inscription for either graph was established. The inspected ZDIC catalogue lists 號 forms from Western Zhou bronzes, while a search result claims a Warring States first appearance; this disagreement needs primary catalogue verification.
No original tiger-roar pictograph image was inspected. The Wiktionary tiger-plus-exhalation account is a secondary proposal and is not independently confirmed here.

The semantic transitions from call/cry to name or title, command, sign/mark, number/order, and classifier are dictionary summaries rather than a fully dated semantic history. Earliest occurrence of each later sense remains to be traced in dated primary texts.
The pronunciation role of 丂 in the graph 号 is not established by the sources inspected. MOE supports the traditional breath-obstruction gloss of 丂, not its phonetic function in 号.

Zhengzhang values for 号 and 號 support a phonetic relationship within 號, but an inspectable primary reconstruction dataset was not opened; other reconstruction systems, including Baxter-Sagart, were not verified.

No sound-based whole-graph loan is proposed or evidenced. The tiger-as-semantic-component interpretation does not require recovery of a distinct historical tiger-call word, and its pictographic origin remains uncertain.

No glyph image is proposed: searches and page inspections did not establish a historical 号/號 image with usable, specific identity and reuse provenance. SFTJ supplied useful labels but direct image fetches failed and its terms did not establish reuse rights; Commons surfaced unrelated or modern drawings.

Xiaoxuetang’s general rights page clearly grants CC0 for query-interface glyph images, but its exact-character query could not be inspected in this session. No candidate image URL or label was supplied by the invocation.
CText's Shuowen page returned 403. MOE reproduces the Shuowen explanations, and ZDIC provides the 號 entry and later commentary; no claim of direct inspection of a Shuowen facsimile is made.

No oracle-bone attestation for either graph was established. The separate 号 catalogue gives Warring States Chu evidence; the 號 catalogue lists Western Zhou bronze evidence. These graph-specific catalogues differ from broad statements that one form is the origin of the other.

The tiger-roar account for 號 is a traditional component interpretation, not proof of an original tiger-call word or recoverable pronunciation for a depicted object. No whole-graph phonetic loan is proposed.

Semantic extensions from cry/call to summons, title/name, command, mark/sign, sequence number, classifier, and other senses are not fully dated. Cited classical work dates do not date surviving manuscripts, and dictionary gloss lists do not establish chronology.

The sources support 口+丂 as the Shuowen account for 号 and an obstructed-breath meaning for 丂; they do not establish 丂 as a sound component of the independent 号 graph. No pronunciation role is assigned to 丂.

Old Chinese and Middle Chinese comparisons for 號 and 号 come from inspected Wiktionary transcriptions attributed to Zhengzhang and Baxter–Sagart, not an independently opened primary dataset. No claim is made that those comparisons establish a tiger-call loan.
